newsitem.title: RUSSIA: China's Jiang set to start visit to Russia.
newsitem.headline: China's Jiang set to start visit to Russia.

text.p: Chinese President Jiang Zemin starts a five-day visit to Russia on Tuesday aimed at building ties between two giants which view each other as key strategic partners in the next century.

President Boris Yeltsin will briefly interrupt his vacation in the Black Sea resort of Sochi to hold talks with Jiang and sign with him a political declaration outlining a joint vision of the future world order.

Jiang, Yeltsin and the presidents of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan will also sign a treaty on reducing armed forces along the former Soviet-Chinese border. Details of the treaty have not been made public.

Russia, deeply unhappy about NATO's plans to expand eastwards, is looking for new allies elsewhere in the world and China, under heavy pressure from the West over human rights violations, is among the most attractive candidates.
Moscow and Beijing have made clear they are poised to set an example for other countries on how to maintain security and build bilateral ties.

"This new type of relationship includes a refusal to take part in military blocs, ruling out confrontation and lack of menace to third parties," Interfax news agency quoted Chinese ambassador to Moscow Li Fenglin as saying on Monday.

Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said the bilateral political declaration, the first such document signed since Moscow and Beijing started repairing ties in the late 1980s after more than two decades of hostility, was very important.

"In this declaration...Russia and China will express their vision of how to form the new international order in the 21st century and will speak out against claims by any country to the role of absolute leader," he told Interfax.
He did not name any state but both Moscow and Beijing have been critical of Washington's domination of the post-Cold War world order.

Apart from political benefits, Moscow clearly hopes for better trade relations with Beijing that would bring greater access to the vast Chinese market and to markets in South-East Asia and the Pacific Rim.
But it also has to solve a number of tricky issues if the current honeymoon with Beijing is to continue.
Itar-Tass news agency said that two-way trade reached $6.9 billion in 1996, 25 percent more than the previous year. But the balance is lop-sided in Russia's favour to the tune of around $3.5 billion.
Moscow officials have said that trade turnover could reach $8-10 billion in 1997 and $20 billion by the end of the century.
Russia hopes to boost arms sales to China from current levels of around $1 billion a year. Some estimates say this could be up to 30 percent of Moscow's overall arms exports.
The two countries, however, have yet to finalise the demarcation of their long border.
The Kremlin has faced angry protests from influential leaders of its Far Eastern regions who say a new proposed borderline is unjust and insist that it be reviewed.
Government officials have dismissed their complaints, saying the demarcation will go ahead as planned.
